input.raw_text: Lumber is the wildest trade in commodities right now. Futures printed a record above $1,700 per thousand board feet this week, roughly four times where they sat a year ago, and sawmills cannot ship fast enough. North American production is running full tilt after last year's curtailments, but it isn't close to enough: the pandemic DIY renovation boom, near-record housing starts, and dealers restocking like mad have emptied the pipeline. Freight and labor shortages at the mills add friction, and Canada's beetle-killed timber hangs over longer-term supply. Homebuilders are swallowing margin as framing packages add thirty thousand dollars or more to a typical new home, and NAHB keeps screaming about it. The scary part is that nobody I talk to sees inventories rebuilding before summer, and anyone short this market has been steamrolled. Mean reversion keeps getting predicted and keeps not showing up.
input.summary: Lumber futures reached a record above $1,700 per thousand board feet, roughly four times their year-earlier level, as renovation activity, near-record housing starts, and dealer restocking outpaced full-capacity North American production. Freight and labor shortages further constrained near-term availability, while beetle-damaged Canadian timber presented a longer-term supply concern. Elevated framing costs pressured homebuilder margins, inventories were not expected to rebuild before summer, and anticipated price normalization had yet to emerge.

citations.text: model_weighting When the multi-asset trend following state is classified as active, emphasize: (1) diversified TSMOM signals across all available asset classes (commodities, equities, fixed income, currencies) to capture the ~4.7x diversification benefit relative to individual-asset Sharpe; (2) volatility-scaled position sizing per instrument (target 10% annualized vol per instrument before combination, consistent with the Hurst et al. benchmark methodology); (3) smile-pattern conditioning: weight TSMOM signals more heavily when trailing equity market returns indicate a sustained directional regime (both bull and bear tails), and reduce weight in trendless high-volatility environments. De-emphasize TSMOM signals when the market is in a mean- reverting choppy regime incompatible with sustained directional moves. The gross diversified TSMOM Sharpe of ~1.8 (January 1985–June 2012) is the benchmark for a fully diversified implementation with proper volatility scaling. Models should not use individual-asset Sharpe ratios (0.29–0.38) as the expected portfolio Sharpe; the diversification benefit is essential. After applying 2-and-20 fee structures, the net-of-fee alpha becomes negative (see failure_hurst_mf_fee_erosion_003); a low-cost systematic implementation (e.g., factor-based) is required to capture meaningful net investor return. Highest confidence in the TSMOM state when: the equity market is in a sustained directional regime (consistent with the smile pattern); the portfolio is diversified across all four asset classes with proper vol-scaling; and implementation costs are below the 6% annual fee-load threshold that eliminates net alpha. The ~1.8 gross Sharpe is computed over January 1985–June 2012 (a 27-year sample dominated by a secular bond bull market and multiple sustained equity bear and bull markets). The volatility target normalization (10% per instrument) is central to achieving the diversification benefit; without it, single-asset concentration dominates. Near-zero S&P 500 correlation (~-0.02) is the key portfolio construction argument for institutional allocation.

matched_states.state_summary: A market condition in which time-series momentum (TSMOM) signals deliver persistent risk-adjusted excess returns across diversified multi-asset futures portfolios. Characterized by: (1) individual-asset Sharpe ratios that increase monotonically with signal look-back horizon—0.29 (1-month), 0.36 (3-month), 0.38 (12-month)—averaged across 58 liquid futures contracts; (2) a diversified 58-instrument TSMOM portfolio achieving ~1.8 gross annualized Sharpe at 10% vol target (January 1985–June 2012); (3) a "smile" return pattern—best performance in sustained trending environments (strong bull or bear markets), worst in trendless choppy markets—with near-zero S&P 500 correlation (~-0.02); (4) after controlling for a simple diversified TSMOM factor, all managed futures fund net-of-fee alphas become negative under 2-and-20 fee structures (~6% average annual fee drag). Most CTAs exhibit dominant exposure to the 3-month TSMOM signal rather than the individually optimal 12-month horizon, and systematically overweight fixed income. Evidence from Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen (2013/2010), evidence_tier 2 (practitioner paper with direct empirical content).
matched_states.title: Multi-Asset Time-Series Momentum Trend Following State
